```json
{
  "winner": "B",
  "reasons": [
    "The 90-day goal is one paying customer, not a defensible business. B's product is narrow (incidents, components, subscriber emails, a public page), sold self-serve at a sourced $9–$29/mo price point, and has a low adoption barrier. A buyer can sign up and pay without integrating anything into their build pipeline.",
    "B has sourced evidence of willingness to pay in the exact format proposed. The r/SaaS thread complains that the market leader charges $399/mo for a manually updated page, and Instatus is cited as reaching ~$10k MRR in this category. A's demand evidence documents that flaky tests hurt. It shows no one paying, or wanting to pay, for an LLM-based selector.",
    "A's own brief names blockers that cut directly against a fast first sale. Buyers need months of track record before letting an AI tool gate merges, and a false negative destroys trust. New installs face a cold-start problem with no test history to learn from. The category skews toward contact-sales enterprise deals (Develocity has no public pricing), and enterprise customers will likely require a DPA and security review before granting access to their codebase.",
    "A's differentiation looks weaker than B's. The brief concedes the core technique doesn't need an LLM, and free OSS clones (ci-sherlock-agent, flaketriage, flaky-detector-agent) plus Testhide's free self-hosted tier already cover it. B also faces a free competitor (OneUptime), but its buyers have documented pricing pain with incumbents, which gives a cheaper entrant a concrete wedge.",
    "Both briefs rest on an unverified six-week build estimate. In A it is explicitly marked [unsourced]. In B it is asserted without a source. So neither gets credit for build speed. The comparison is decided on payer friction and demand evidence, where B is stronger."
  ],
  "weakest_evidence_in_loser": "A's headline demand quote comes from Federico, a TLM at Trunk, describing Trunk's own flaky-test tool in a Trunk-authored HackerNoon article. That makes it vendor marketing, not independent buyer demand. It shows awareness of the problem, not willingness to pay a new solo vendor. A's price hypothesis is also weak: it is anchored to Harness's general AI Dev Assistant add-on rather than any priced test-selection product, while the closest direct competitor, Develocity, publishes no price.",
  "confidence_note": "Moderate-to-low confidence. Both briefs describe saturated markets with free alternatives, and neither has direct evidence that a new entrant has won a first paying customer quickly. B's main weaknesses are a $0 competitor (OneUptime), an SEO channel already occupied by Hyperping, and slow growth for the Instatus proof point (~$500/mo MRR added). These make it a poor long-term bet but a more plausible first sale than A. A's trust, cold-start, and integration barriers are specific to getting someone to pay at all within 90 days. The pick would flip if A had evidence that teams pay for advisory-only flaky-test flagging with no gating."
}
```
